# Memory and locality {style="text-align: center;"}

## The memory hierarchy

. . .

| Level | Typical capacity | Typical latency |
|---|---|---|
| Registers | < 1 KiB per core | none |
| L1 | 32–64 KiB per core | ~1 ns |
| L2 | 256 KiB–2 MiB | ~4 ns |
| L3 | 8–32 MiB | ~15 ns |
| RAM | 16–64 GiB | ~100 ns |

. . .

> The core looks in L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Smaller memories are closer to the core.

::: {.notes}
Indicative orders of magnitude, not specifications for every processor. Registers: x86-64 has
16 general-purpose 64-bit registers and 16 vector registers (256 bits with AVX2, as on the
reference laptop). Cache sharing differs by level and core design. Reference laptop: 24 MiB
shared L3; L1d 544 KiB in 14 instances, L2 18 MiB in 9 instances. Do not interpret aggregate
cache sizes as a single core's cache.
Access latency is not the mean time per element in a streaming loop.
:::

## Who decides where data live?

- **Registers:** the compiler. In `s += a[i]`, the local variable `s` stays in a register.
- **L1, L2, L3:** the hardware, automatically. No instruction says "keep this array in L2".
- **You:** indirectly, through access order, data size and reuse.

. . .

> On a GPU, part of this is explicit: a fast on-chip **shared memory** is managed by the programmer.

::: {.notes}
When registers run out, the compiler "spills" variables to the stack, which in practice lives in L1.
The compiler inspection of module 1 (optional section) shows the accumulator in a register (xmm/ymm).
Expert hints exist but are out of scope: prefetch instructions, stores that bypass the cache,
cache partitioning on servers. The two experiments of this deck act on access order and reuse.
GPU (NVIDIA): registers per thread, shared memory per block of threads (explicit, e.g.
CuStaticSharedArray in CUDA.jl), global memory = VRAM, plus automatic L1/L2 caches. Not used in
this course. A warp is a group of 32 threads executing together, not a memory level.
:::

## Two forms of locality

. . .

| Locality | Practical idea | Experiment |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial | Use neighboring values | Loop order |
| Temporal | Reuse recently accessed values | Batching |

. . .

> On the reference machine, a 64-byte cache line holds **eight Float64 values**.

::: {.notes}
A cache line is a transfer unit, not one individual array entry. Temporal reuse depends on
working-set size and access order; merely repeating a computation does not ensure a cache hit.
:::

## Repeated sums as the array grows

. . .

Sum an array repeatedly, varying its footprint from **8 KiB to 64 MiB**.

```julia
for _ in 1:passes
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(a)
        s += a[i]
    end
end
```

. . .

> Predict how the **average time per element** changes with array size.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "1. Repeated sums as the array grows". Keep approximately the same total number
of element visits. The metric is elapsed time divided by passes × length(a). It is an
aggregate processing-rate measurement, not a dependent-load latency measurement.
Show selected footprints rather than the entire sweep.
:::

## Array size and processing rate

. . .

Reference observations on the course laptop:

| Footprint | Average ns / element |
|---|---|
| 8 KiB | 0.049 |
| 4 MiB | 0.128 |
| 64 MiB | 0.317 |

. . .

> A larger working set changes the processing rate. These numbers are **not individual access latencies**.

::: {.notes}
Historical rounded BenchmarkTools minimum timings normalized by all processed elements.
The reference L3 is 24 MiB. Cache capacity, prefetching, vectorization and other hardware
behavior contribute. Do not assign every point to one cache level from timing alone.
:::

## Latency is not time per element {#latency}

- **Latency:** delay until one requested value is available.
- **Transfer unit:** RAM sends a whole cache line (64 bytes) in one burst over the **bus** (the wires between RAM and the chip), a few bytes per step.
- **Processing rate:** in an in-order scan, the CPU requests the next lines before they are needed, so the waits overlap.

. . .

> Average time per element can be much smaller than access latency.

::: {.notes}
One wait of ~100 ns brings 8 Float64. At 64 MiB we measure 0.317 ns per element, i.e. ~25 GB/s
for one core; with ~100 ns latency that needs ~2.5 KB, i.e. ~40 cache lines, in flight at once
(rate × latency). The prefetchers keep that many requests going.
Analogy: order many pizzas at once instead of waiting for each one; every delivery still takes
30 minutes (latency), but one arrives every minute (rate).
Bus width depends on the memory type; the line is always 64 bytes. DDR4: 64-bit channel, 8
transfers per line. DDR5: 32-bit subchannels, 16 transfers. Reference laptop: LPDDR5 at 7467 MT/s,
8 channels of 16 bits, so 32 transfers of 2 bytes per line, ~120 GB/s peak over all channels.
Do not confuse with a "64-bit processor": that is the width of registers and addresses (a Float64
fits in one register). The CPU–GPU link of the GPU module (PCIe) is another link.
Prefetching and multiple outstanding accesses can hide latency in a stream. A dependent
pointer-chasing traversal is another experiment; random addresses alone do not necessarily
prevent overlapping reads. Later, distinguish per-request latency from examples per second.
:::

# Experiment 1 — use neighboring data {style="text-align: center;"}

## Two loop orders, the same sum

. . .

Sum an 8000×8000 matrix, two loop orders:

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# COLUMN by column
for j in axes(M, 2)
    for i in axes(M, 1)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```julia
# ROW by row
for i in axes(M, 1)
    for j in axes(M, 2)
        s += M[i, j]
    end
end
```
:::
::::

. . .

> Which order is faster? Predict before measuring.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "2. Locality — the same sum, walked two ways". Julia dense column-major matrix.
The sum is mathematically unchanged, but floating-point rounding can depend on the addition order.
:::

## Loop order and memory layout {#a4-debrief}

. . .

Reference: Julia, **8000² Float64 ≈ 488 MiB**.

| Walk | Time | Access pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Columns | 30.4 ms | Consecutive values |
| Rows | 361.4 ms | Large strides |

. . .

> Contiguous accesses make better use of cache lines and prefetching.

::: {.notes}
Historical rounded minimum timings on the course laptop: about 11.9× in this case.
The timings do not establish that each noncontiguous cache line supplies exactly one value
before eviction. Julia dense matrices are column-major; the Python activity uses C-contiguous
arrays, so the preferred inner index differs. Array views can have other stride patterns.
:::

## Test the effect of matrix size

. . .

If locality matters, how should the difference change for a smaller matrix?

. . .

| Matrix | Footprint | Rows / columns |
|---|---|---|
| 100² | 78 KiB | 0.9× |
| 4000² | 122 MiB | 7.2× |

. . .

> The difference is small **here** when the matrix fits in cache.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "Test the effect of matrix size". Historical reference observations.
The size-dependent gap supports a locality explanation; it does not isolate cache effects
from prefetching and translation costs, or guarantee that loop order stops mattering in cache.
Collect a prediction before revealing the table. Compare with smaller inputs in the activity.
:::

# Experiment 2 — reuse data {style="text-align: center;"}

## One example or a batch?

. . .

```julia
y = W * x     # one example
Y = W * X     # B examples, stored as columns
```

Batching lets matrix multiplication **reuse weights across examples**.

. . .

> `W`: 4096² Float32 = **64 MiB**. What happens to the time per example as `B` increases?

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "3. Batching: one layer W, B examples". Actual traffic depends on tiling, caches
and implementation; do not say each weight is loaded exactly once per batch.
The reference is a true matrix-vector product W*x, not a one-column matrix product.
The demonstration reports time per batch and per example; the activity holds the total number
of examples fixed. Both compare with individual matrix-vector products.
:::

## Batching: measured speedups {#a5-debrief}

. . .

Reference, `W` = 64 MiB: **`W * x` = 1090 µs per example**.

| B | ms / batch | µs / example | Speedup vs `W*x` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 5.65 | 706.0 | 1.5× |
| 64 | 11.06 | 172.9 | 6.3× |
| 256 | 39.06 | 152.6 | 7.1× |
| 1024 | 141.80 | 138.5 | 7.9× |

. . .

> Compare the trend with your measurements. Larger batches give **diminishing returns** here.

::: {.notes}
Historical rounded BenchmarkTools minimum timings on the course laptop, not new measurements. The reference is
single-vector GEMV. B=1 as a one-column matrix product took 2551.8 µs in this run; it is
intentionally omitted to avoid confusing it with the 1090-µs vector reference.
The activity uses a smaller W (4 MiB), fixed BLAS threads and the same total of 128 examples.
A gain can remain even if W fits in L3: cache reuse at other levels and call overhead also matter.
A plateau alone does not identify the limiting resource. Vary dimensions and BLAS threads to test it.
:::

## Choosing the batch size

- **Throughput:** larger batches can reduce time per example.
- **Latency:** requests may wait for the batch to fill **and finish**.
- **Memory:** larger batches need larger input/output buffers.

. . .

> Choose the smallest batch that meets throughput and latency targets within the memory budget.

::: {.notes}
For offline work choose a batch near the best observed throughput without unnecessary buffers.
The activity's input/output payload per batch is a model, not a measurement of peak process RAM:
the full dataset is already resident and concatenation also allocates memory. Queueing time is
not measured by the matrix-product timer.
An optional simplified model is t_example ≈ t_compute + t_load/B. It suggests amortization,
but does not identify which term dominates or prove compute-bound execution.
:::

## Three practical choices

:::{.nonincremental}
- Follow the array's **memory layout**.
- **Reuse data** across computations.
- Choose batch size by measuring **throughput, latency and memory use**.
:::

# Optional references {#appendix style="text-align: center;"}

## Library routines can adapt to layout

. . .

Compare an explicit **compiled loop** with a library reduction on the same array layouts.

| Operation | Reference observation |
|---|---|
| NumPy `A.sum(axis=0)`, C vs F order | Similar times in this run |
| Copy F→C versus C→C | 109.5 versus 8.3 ms |

. . .

> Inspect the layout and measure the **operation**; library routines need not follow your loop order.

::: {.notes}
Python notebook: compiled locality loops, then this optional library/layout comparison.
The historical 8000² reduction ratio was about 1×; a mismatched copy was 13.2× slower.
Those are observations, not properties of all NumPy reductions. A library can choose traversal
and blocking strategies; the comparison is explicit loops versus optimized routines, not Python
versus Julia. Views and strides still matter. Verify outputs within tolerance before timing.
:::

## Reuse output buffers when beneficial

. . .

```julia
z = 2 .* x .+ y      # allocate an output array
z .= 2 .* x .+ y     # reuse the existing output
```

| Reference, n = 10⁷ | Time | Allocated |
|---|---|---|
| New output | 54 ms | 76 MiB |
| Reused output | 17 ms | 0 bytes |

. . .

> Reuse avoids an allocation; the computation still **reads and writes data**.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "Optional — reuse output buffers". Historical rounded minimum timings.
Compare with mul!(C,A,B) versus A*B. Gains depend on output size, allocation strategy and
traffic; pooling can make allocation cheap. Zero allocated bytes does not mean zero memory
traffic. NumPy out= operations can reuse buffers, but separate calls are not generally fused.
:::

## Arithmetic intensity: FLOP per byte

. . .

Idealized Float64 traffic, ignoring lower-order terms:

| Operation | FLOP | Bytes | FLOP / byte |
|---|---|---|---|
| n×n matrix × vector | 2n² | ~8n² | ~0.25 |
| n×n matrix × matrix | 2n³ | ~24n² | ~n/12 |

. . .

> Use **GFLOP/s** to compare computational throughput.

::: {.notes}
▶ Script: cell "Optional — arithmetic intensity". FLOP denotes a floating-point operation.
Actual traffic depends on cache reuse and the implementation. Intensity is a model of work
per byte, not a measured bandwidth. Timing still matters for application latency; GFLOP/s
normalizes different amounts of arithmetic for a throughput comparison.
:::
